chapter_theme: Poems 321-340 praise the small warrior villages of hard, dry land (vaakai: வல்லாண் முல்லை and மூதின் முல்லை), whose chiefs and wives give away even their seed grain and whose only god is the hero-stone, then turn to the magatpaal kaanchi poems, where a king's demand for a chief's daughter brings war on her town.

321.reading: The bard is told that the town guarded by the battle-loving lord whose head bears sword scars lies in hard country, where a fighting quail snatches husked sesame drying on a winnowing tray and, chased by a rat with ears like a summer kongu bud, hides in the thick millet stalks.
321.nuance: The long opening shows a poor dry land where even a quail must steal grain and hide, so the town's strength is all in its lord: the poem turns from a small comic chase to the scarred head in the last two lines. Line 8 is broken, so what the bard is told to do on arrival (eat fruit and rest?) is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem ends on the lord's battle scars and love of war, the valour of a small-land chief

322.reading: The spearman who denies sleep to the kings of the cool wet fields lives in hard country, where dull-headed boys leaning on cactus with thorns like an old plough-bull's worn horns watch for rats in the millet stubble and their shouts send a hare leaping across the common, breaking the black pots, while near by, when the sugarcane press groans, the vaalai fish leap.
322.nuance: Two economies sit side by side: boys hunting rats in a dry millet land, and the sugar mills and fish of the kings' watered fields next door. The hero belongs to the poor land, and his threat runs from it to the rich one.

thinai_evidence.note: the praise is of a spearman whose threat keeps kings awake

comparisons.tenor: the forked thorns of the cactus

323.reading: An old cow, her anger gone, suckles the calf of a wild cow that a tiger has taken, and (after a broken line) the poem praises the spearman's unguarded giving that flows to whatever is wished for, and his sword, which leaves its sheath only for elephants.
323.nuance: The image of a cow nursing an orphan of another kind is set before ஓம்பா ஈகை, giving that keeps nothing back; line 3, which would have joined them, is lost, so whether it was an open simile cannot be known.

thinai_evidence.note: generosity and a sword kept for elephants alone, the paired virtues of the small-land hero

comparisons.tenor: the hero's giving to those not his own

324.reading: In a small village on poor land, where hunters' boys with frightened eyes like a wild tomcat's and mouths smelling of bird meat bend their bows with thorn-tipped reed arrows to watch for rats at the cotton hedge, the modest noble man who sits with the bards by a herdsman's small fire is the heart-knowing companion of the victorious king, who will perish when the king perishes.
324.nuance: The hero is first shown at ease, modest among bards in a poor village; his value is stated only at the end and as a pledge, not a deed. Lines 9 and 10 (what spreads over the pandal) are obscure.

thinai_evidence.note: the hero is praised as the king's companion unto death

325.reading: In a dry settlement where cows take turns drinking the muddy seep of a dug pit after a stray rain has passed, where the porcupine hunters' share of fat burning on the firebrand scents the street and boys play at arrows under the jujube's swaying shade, stands the thorn-fenced town of the lord of unbounded giving, who will hold back even a king who comes at the head of a victorious army.
325.nuance: The pun in the last lines turns on one verb: தாங்கும், he holds back the king, and தாங்கா ஈகை, giving that cannot be held back. The rain is வம்ப, untimely, and leaves only a muddy pit, so the land is shown as poor in water before it is praised.

thinai_evidence.note: the lord resists kings and gives without limit

326.reading: In a thorn-fenced village where a young hen, terrified by the wild cat that prowls the old hedge, cries until the cotton-spinning woman rises with her small lamp and it calms beside the crested cock, the wife longs to feast arriving guests and bards on curd-rice with iguana fat, and her husband, who shattered the enemy in hard battle, owns the great gift of the gold forehead plate from the leading elephant.
326.nuance: The frightened hen that quiets beside the cock may be read as a quiet figure of the village safe beside its warrior, though the poem draws no comparison. The wife's wish that the hunting boys not go far is a wish to have meat ready for guests, so even the hunt serves hospitality.

thinai_evidence.note: the old warrior house: the wife's hospitality and the husband's battle gift

327.reading: After the creditors took their share of a meagre millet crop threshed by hand without oxen and the hungry bards ate the rest, the noble man, to end his people's want, goes to the small farmers of his own town and begs millet face to face; and this is the strong man who holds back any king who comes.
327.nuance: The poem sets the begging and the valour in one sentence, so the man who stoops to ask small farmers for grain is the same man who will stand against a king; begging is not shame when it is for others.

thinai_evidence.note: the poor hero's begging for others and his strength against kings

328.reading: In a small village of poor land by the woods where no paddy grows and all its millet and thinai have gone in gifts to suppliants, the bard is told that the little king, though so reduced, will still cook dried meat and fresh rice in ghee for him and give him gifts if he goes singing to the yard where hares nibble the fragrant muññai.
328.nuance: Lines 1, 5, 7 to 9, 12 and 13 are broken; the sense of the whole (an empty granary, yet a feast promised) survives, but the details of the meal and of line 5 do not.

thinai_evidence.note: giving that outlasts the village's grain

comparisons.tenor: a dish of the meal; the tenor is lost in the gap of line 8

329.reading: Though the small village of a few houses that brew their own toddy sits at a dangerous frontier, where the hero-stone at its edge gets daily offerings, is bathed and lit with ghee and its dark smoke spreads like mist down the street, and though it is as hard to approach as an anthill where a striped cobra lives, the famed noble man who guards it gives to suppliants every day without stint.
329.nuance: The anthill simile faces two ways: to enemies the village is a snake's hole, to suppliants it is open every day. The phrase in line 7 about the patron's distress is not certain: it may mean that he gives without minding what giving costs him.

thinai_evidence.note: constant giving in a dangerous frontier village

comparisons.tenor: the frontier village, dangerous to approach

330.reading: When a king's army pressed in and broke the front, he stood alone with raised sword and stopped it from passing him, as the shore stops the great sea; and always, beyond what he gave those who came singing, his generosity keeps up the old name of a small village too poor to pay its levy.
330.nuance: ஆழி here is the shore or boundary that the sea cannot pass, so the army becomes the sea; the image measures one man against a whole host.

thinai_evidence.note: a single warrior's stand and his giving

comparisons.tenor: the lone warrior holding back the army

331.reading: The strength of a small village that lives by the bow, with a well cut through rock, is a chief who, though very poor, can make what is not there, like an unlearned herdsman kindling a small fire on a cold evening; can measure out in order to a few, like a good housewife who serves a long pandal of guests from very little without saying they are too many; and, when he scatters gifts, can scatter them like the white rice of offering cast at the gates of guarding kings.
331.nuance: The three similes are a scale of giving: making something from nothing, sharing scarcity fairly, and pouring out freely. All three vehicles are humble or domestic, a herdsman and a housewife set beside the king's offering rice.

thinai_evidence.note: the poor chief's skill in giving

comparisons.tenor: the chief contriving what he lacks
the chief measuring out a little to many

332.reading: Unlike other men's spears, this warrior's spear has its own greatness: sometimes it lies in the thatch of the hut with dust on its dark back; sometimes, garlanded among auspicious women, it is carried round the pond and the streets to the sound of drums and lutes till the land trembles; and it never stops short of the faces of the great elephants of kings whose armies are like the sea.
332.nuance: The spear is given three states, idle, honoured and in battle, and the repeated கிடக்கினும் கிடக்கும் and செல்லினும் செல்லும் make its indifference to the first two a mark of greatness.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the warrior through his spear

333.reading: Poets are urged to stay at a poor village where hares with eyes like raindrop bubbles leap in the bushes of the holed common, even though no one there knows how to say 'eat', for the housewife, her millet and thinai all given to suppliants and no loan coming back, has put the dried seed-millet into the mortar; and her lord, who would face a king with a new-decked elephant, eats only that and gives as gifts what he takes in battle.
333.nuance: Cooking the seed grain is the extreme of hospitality: it spends next year's crop on today's guest. Lines 14 and 15 are broken, and the closing lines (what the lord eats, what he takes as his gift) can be read more than one way.

thinai_evidence.note: the old warrior house that gives away even its seed and faces kings

334.reading: Where hares with fur like the sedge flower hide in the thickets when boys shout on the common, the housewife never rests her hands from the clatter of feeding bards and keeping suppliants, and the young bull-like spearman never rests his either, giving away the gold ornaments taken from the faces of high-tusked elephants.
334.nuance: The poem rhymes the wife and the husband: கைதூ வாளே, she does not rest her hands, and கைதூ வானே, he does not rest his, which makes hospitality and battle-won giving one shared duty of the house. Lines 4, 5 and 9 are broken.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife and the warrior are equally unresting in giving

335.reading: In this land there are only four flowers (kuravam, ..., kuruntham, mullai), only four foods (millet, thinai, horsegram and beans), only four clans (the thudi drummer, the bard, the parai drummer and the kadamban), and no god worshipped with scattered paddy except the stone praised for the warrior who stood against the enemy, struck down a bright-tusked elephant and fell.
335.nuance: The fourfold lists read like a census of a whole way of life, and the last item overturns the pattern: not four gods but one, and that one a man. The first line and a half are broken, so one flower is lost.

thinai_evidence.note: the only god of the land is the fallen warrior's stone

336.reading: The king who wants the girl is hot with anger and her father will not do what is due; the elephants have not yet been tied to the guarded tree, the spearmen who reached it are silent, and with drums sounding that even the musicians do not know, this ancient guarded town is in great turmoil; truly without virtue is the mother who, raising the girl's young breasts with the beauty of kongu buds on the vengai hill, raised enmity along with her.
336.nuance: The blame falls on the mother, not on the king or the father: her care in rearing the girl's beauty is said to have reared a war. Lines 4 and 5 (the guarded tree, the warriors' வாய்மூழ்த்தனரே) are hard, and the state of the siege is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: a king's demand for a daughter brings war on the town

337.reading: Though the Chola lord is loud with power and suitors who rule the earth have come singing, she, like the cold spring on Pari's Parambu, has become hard to see, kept indoors in the tall fragrant house; kings keep coming, feeding paddy to their fierce elephants in every grove, while her brothers' heads are clotted with blood from their long spears, and the poet asks who will ever be the ones to press her young breasts.
337.nuance: Kapilar, Pari's own poet, uses his dead patron's hill spring as the measure of something precious and out of reach. The closing question is not a wish but a threat: given her brothers' spears, it is not clear anyone will live to marry her. Lines 3, 4 and 13 are obscure.

thinai_evidence.note: kings besiege a house to win a daughter her brothers guard

338.reading: Like Neduvel Aathan's Ponthai, rich in ploughed fields, paddy-filled houses, gold-filled streets and bee-loud groves, she is of great worth and hard to win: even if the victorious kings who wear neem, aar and palmyra bring gifts, the king of a single fort, which stands among the paddy fields like a stranded ship in the sea, will not give his one young daughter to any who do not bow as befits him.
338.nuance: The three garlands are the emblems of the Pandya, Chola and Chera, so the refusal is made to all the crowned kings at once by the lord of one fort. போந்தை is both the town of line 4 and the palmyra of line 6.

thinai_evidence.note: a small king refuses his daughter to the three crowned kings

comparisons.tenor: the single fort among the fields

339.reading: Where a long-horned bull rests in the shade, cowherds pluck crowded mullai flowers, a hare struck by a stick leaps among vaalai fish in the flood, and bangled women bathe in the sea, dive in ponds and pick neythal flowers from the backwater, she has grown, and the poet says she has taken and hidden in herself the fierce hearts of kings with winnow-eared elephants who are eager for hard battle.
339.nuance: The opening gathers three landscapes, pasture, wet field and shore, into one country, so the girl is the flower of a land that has everything; the comic hare among the fish marks the floods. Line 10 is lost, and the sense of line 12 is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl draws kings to war

340.reading: To one who asks about the young girl who runs, her leaf skirt swaying, to gather spotted kunri seeds, the speaker answers (through broken lines) that her father has set her apart for great kings whose elephants with trunks like dark palmyras trample the karanthai fields.
340.nuance: The child still playing with seeds is already the subject of kings' wars; the gaps in lines 3 to 6 hide who asks and whose father is meant, and வரைந்திருந்தனனே may mean he has promised her or has limited her to such kings.

thinai_evidence.note: the daughter's marriage is a matter between kings

links.note: Kural 1066 says nothing is more degrading to the tongue than begging, even water for a cow; 327 praises a chief who begs millet face to face from small farmers to feed bards and his kin.
links.teaches: The Kural's limit case (begging even for a good cause is degrading) is exactly what the Purananuru holds up as heroic, so the pair shows that the shame of asking was a later ethical rule, while the older warrior ethic counted begging for others as part of generosity.

links.note: Kural 219 defines the generous man's poverty as being unable to do what he should; 331 says its chief, though very poor, can make what is not there and still give.
links.teaches: Valluvar treats poverty as the one thing that disables the generous man, while the Purananuru poet shows a poor chief whose skill in contriving, rationing and scattering defeats that disablement, so the pair shows generosity measured in the Kural by means and in the poem by craft.

links.note: Kural 85 asks whether the field of a man who feeds guests and eats the leftovers even needs sowing; in 333 the wife has fed guests until she must pound the seed millet itself.
links.teaches: The Kural's rhetorical promise that the hospitable house needs no seed is played out literally in the poem, where hospitality has eaten the seed, so the pair shows the real cost that the maxim's confidence passes over.

links.note: Kural 780 calls a death that makes one's patron weep worth begging for; 324 praises a companion who will die when his king dies.
links.teaches: The Kural places the good death before the lord's, earning his tears, while the poem binds the companion's death to follow the king's, so together they show two orders of loyalty in Tamil war ethics: dying for the lord and dying with him.

links.note: In 95 Avvaiyar contrasts one king's spears, feathered, garlanded and oiled in the palace, with Adiyaman's, their tips broken from use and lying in the smith's shed; 332 gives a single warrior's spear both lives, idle in the hut and garlanded in procession, and then the elephant charge.
links.teaches: Avvaiyar splits the honoured spear and the used spear between two kings to shame one, while 332 joins them in one spear, so the pair shows that the garlanded spear was not itself a mark of idleness; only the spear that never went to battle was.

links.note: Both use the cold spring of Pari's Parambu: in 176 its clear water is neglected by those who live by it; in 337 Kapilar likens the confined girl to it as hard to see.
links.teaches: One famous spring serves two opposite points, a good thing slighted because it is near and a good thing prized because it is out of reach, which shows that Pari's hill had become a shared figure of the precious whose sense each poet could turn.

links.note: Akananuru 60's friend says the mother will keep the girl under closer guard than the Chola treasure and asks the hero not to crush her bangled girl; 337 says the girl is confined to the house (மனைச்செறிந் தனளே) and asks who will crush (ஞெமுக்குவோரே) her young breasts.
links.teaches: The same confinement of the maturing girl and the same verb for the lover's embrace appear in both, but in akam the guard is a mother keeping off one lover while in puram it is brothers with bloody spears keeping off kings, which shows the puram poet enlarging an akam household scene into war.

links.note: Akananuru 60 calls the mother who will guard the girl அறன்இல் யாய்; 336 calls the mother who reared the girl's beauty அறன்இலன் and பண்புஇல் தாய்.
links.teaches: Both poems blame the mother with the same word, but the akam friend blames her for guarding the girl too closely and the puram poet for rearing a beauty that draws war, which shows that the girl's beauty, a private matter in akam, becomes a public danger in the kaanchi poems.

links.note: Akananuru 90's friend says that even the Kosars' town would not be accepted as the price of the girl; 338 says the father will not give his daughter even if the three crowned kings bring gifts, unless they bow.
links.teaches: The akam friend's boast that no price is enough for the girl is the same claim the puram father makes against kings, so the pair shows a shared convention of the priceless daughter that in akam keeps a lover waiting and in puram starts a war.

links.note: In both, the wife feeds bards and guests while the husband gives or holds the gold ornament taken from a war elephant's face.
links.teaches: Two poets build the old warrior house (மூதின் முல்லை) from the same pair of acts, the wife's feeding and the husband's elephant gold, which shows that the thurai required the wife's hospitality as an equal half of the house's heroism.

links.note: 329 shows the village hero-stone given daily offerings, bathed and lit with ghee; 335 says the stone of the warrior who fell killing an elephant is the only god of its land.
links.teaches: 329 shows the rite and 335 states the creed behind it, so the pair shows that in these small warrior villages the hero-stone was not one cult among others but the whole of public worship.

new_concepts.gloss: the gift a bard seeks from a patron, and the asking for it
new_concepts.label_source: the verses use the word: பரிசிலன் in 326 line 15, பரிசில் in 333 line 19, பரிசிலர் and பரிசில் in 334 lines 6 and 10

new_concepts.gloss: a king's demand for a chief's daughter, refused, and the war it brings on the town

source_issues: 323, 327, 328, 333, 339 and 340: the poet is not recorded (poet None).
321 line 8, 323 line 3, 328 lines 1, 5, 7-9, 12-13, 333 lines 14-15, 334 lines 4-5 and 9, 335 lines 1-2, 337 line 4, 339 line 10 and 340 lines 3-6 have dotted gaps; marked as they stand.
323 line 3 and 334 line 9: show flags a word beginning with a dead consonant (க்கு, ப்); each is the tail of a word lost in the gap before it.
325: the review's line table says we lack the site's lines 14 and 15, but our text now has 15 lines ending வேந்து தலைவரினும் தாங்கும், / தாங்கா ஈகை, நெடுந்தகை ஊரே; the table row looks out of date.
336: the review says our colophon read பாற் பாற் காஞ்சி; show now prints மகட்பாற் காஞ்சி, so it appears corrected.

338: the review says the site lacks our line 1 (ஏர் பரந்த வயல், நீர் பரந்த செறுவின்); it begins the list of the town's wealth that போந்தை அன்ன (line 4) closes, so it belongs to the poem; marked as it stands.
321 is listed in the review among poems with stray non-Tamil glyphs; the text show prints has none.
331: the poet field carries a variant in brackets (உறையூர் முது கூற்றனார் எனவும் பாடம்).
